options.text: Magnification = Actual size x Image size

questions.explanation: The magnification formula is M = I / A (Magnification = Image size divided by Actual size). This can be rearranged to find any of the three values.

questions.stem: How many micrometres (um) are in 1 millimetre (mm)?
questions.explanation: There are 1,000 micrometres in 1 millimetre. To convert mm to um, multiply by 1,000.

questions.stem: A cell has an actual diameter of 50 um. In a microscope image, it measures 20 mm. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: First convert to the same units: 20 mm = 20,000 um. Then M = I/A = 20,000/50 = x400.

questions.explanation: Magnification is a ratio of image size to actual size, so it has no units. We write it as x400, but the 'x' simply means 'times', not a unit.

questions.stem: A microscope image of a bacterium measures 3 mm long at x2,000 magnification. What is the actual length?
questions.explanation: Convert image size: 3 mm = 3,000 um. Then A = I/M = 3,000/2,000 = 1.5 um.

questions.stem: How many nanometres (nm) are in 1 micrometre (um)?
questions.explanation: There are 1,000 nanometres in 1 micrometre. To convert um to nm, multiply by 1,000.

questions.stem: What is a scale bar on a micrograph used for?

options.text: To show how colourful the specimen is
To determine the actual size of structures in the image
To measure the magnification of the eyepiece lens

questions.explanation: A scale bar on a micrograph shows what distance on the image corresponds to an actual measurement. It allows you to calculate the magnification and determine actual sizes of structures.
